prompt: A service expects 24,000 requests per day. Each request averages 2 model calls with 1,200 input and 300 output tokens per call. Which estimate is the correct starting point before selecting a route?

options.text: 24,000 calls and 36 million total tokens per day, because each user request is one model call.
48,000 calls/day, 57.6 million input tokens/day, and 14.4 million output tokens/day, then apply route/model prices and operational headroom.
48,000 calls/day and 72 million input tokens/day because input and output tokens have the same volume.
24,000 calls/day and 14.4 million output tokens/day, then select the lowest advertised input-token price.

feedback.reason: Multiply expected requests by calls per request, then calculate input and output tokens separately before applying the selected model/route rates.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Call volume, input volume, and output volume are separate cost/capacity drivers; a per-request estimate that omits internal calls understates demand.

prompt: A claims workflow needs perfect enforcement of a statutory eligibility rule, exact lookup of current policy status, and natural-language explanation of ambiguous evidence. The model is fast and the expected monthly token cost is acceptable. What is the correct feasibility verdict?

options.text: Feasible end to end because the expected cost and latency meet budget.
Infeasible in every form because Claude cannot participate in a workflow with legal rules.
Feasible only as an assistant: use authoritative system state and deterministic rule enforcement for eligibility, while the model interprets ambiguous evidence and explains the result under review.
Feasible if the system prompt repeats the eligibility rule and the model’s refusal behavior is used as the legal control.

feedback.reason: The four-property assessment includes whether nondeterministic, steerable generation can satisfy a hard correctness requirement; the solution can be scoped around deterministic systems and human review.

prompt: A multilingual support bot is judged feasible because its average answer quality clears target. In one language, however, wrong account actions occur in 3% of cases and the action must be exact. What is the strongest next decision?

options.text: Proceed with the model because the overall average is above target and add a generic disclaimer.
Increase the sample size across all languages but keep the same overall average as the release criterion.
Ask the model to mention uncertainty after it selects an account action.
Set a language-specific minimum on the exact action outcome; test route/model or deterministic controls for that slice and keep it out of autonomous action until it clears the boundary.

feedback.reason: An aggregate mean can conceal a high-consequence slice failure; feasibility needs a scoped boundary where deterministic correctness is required.

prompt: A 10% exception class needs 12 model calls per case and a deep context; the other 90% needs one short call and has a strict latency budget. Which feasibility approach best preserves the business objective?

options.text: Size the routine and exception populations separately; keep the proven one-call routine path and test whether the exception workflow can meet its distinct cost, context, and latency boundaries before expanding it.
Adopt the exception workflow for all requests so the architecture has one implementation and one average cost.
Judge feasibility from the blended average call count and total monthly budget only.
Remove the exception cases from measurement because they are too rare to affect feasibility.

feedback.reason: Separate workload classes because an average can hide an infeasible exception path or unnecessarily burden the routine majority.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A scoped architecture can use different patterns or explicit boundaries for distinct workload shapes.

details.transfer: Define workload segments, measure their distinct cost and quality, and make a clear in-scope/out-of-scope decision.
